text: Chunce is present for the Big Bang and files it as a noise complaint.
Chunce reports on the formation of the Earth and describes it as "still settling."
Chunce warns the dinosaurs about an approaching object. The dinosaurs, having no readership, are unmoved.
Chunce watches an early human pick up the first stone tool and asks whether it has been risk-assessed.
Chunce attends the first known musical performance, on a bone flute, and leaves at the interval.
Chunce contributes to the Lascaux cave paintings. Experts have since identified his section as "mostly signature."
Chunce attends the opening of Göbekli Tepe and notes that it has made no provision for parking.
Chunce reports on the invention of farming and predicts that it will lead to paperwork. He is correct.
Chunce is given a tour of the walls of Jericho and describes them as "solid, for now."
Doggerland floods and Britain becomes an island. Chunce, who had a house there, blames the council.
Writing is invented in Sumer. Chunce, who has been writing for some time, asks what took everyone so long.
Chunce covers the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt and asks which one is which. Nobody is certain.
Chunce is buried alongside a pharaoh as a precaution. He files his copy from inside the tomb regardless.
Silbury Hill is completed. Nobody can say what it is for, and Chunce, who can, refuses on principle.
Sargon of Akkad offers Chunce an empire in exchange for favourable coverage. Chunce declines, citing editorial independence and the size of the empire.
Chunce reads Hammurabi's Code in full and notes that it contains nothing about misquoting a source.
Chunce covers the Battle of Kadesh. The Egyptians and the Hittites both claim victory, and both quote him in support.
Chunce reports on the collapse of the Bronze Age and blames the Sea Peoples, who decline to give a surname.
Chunce attends the founding of Rome and asks Romulus whether his brother would like to comment. He would not.
Homer completes the Odyssey. Chunce, who got home from Troy in a fortnight by the direct route, calls it padded.
Chunce interviews a tortoise after its race with a hare and is told that it was "never about the result."
Thales predicts a solar eclipse. Chunce, who predicted it several thousand years earlier, is not credited.
Chunce reports that Babylon is impregnable, shortly before Cyrus walks in along the river bed.
Chunce attends the birth of democracy in Athens and immediately demands a recount.
Sun Tzu completes The Art of War. Chunce, who shared a tent with him, says it could have been more concise.
Chunce asks the Spartans at Thermopylae whether they have considered a different pass.
Chunce reviews the new Parthenon and suggests it would look better with more roof. It later ends up with less.
Herodotus is named the Father of History. Chunce asks who, in that case, is the grandfather.
Chunce enrols at Plato's Academy and is asked to leave the cave, the allegory and the building.
Chunce asks Diogenes for a comment. Diogenes asks him to stand out of his light.
Chunce asks Alexander the Great what he will do once there is nothing left to conquer. Alexander weeps. Chunce files it as a yes.
Euclid publishes his Elements. Chunce asks whether any of it is news.
Chunce donates his memoirs to the Library of Alexandria. They take up three wings.
Archimedes runs naked through Syracuse shouting about bathwater. Chunce, who had been waiting for the bath, lodges a complaint.
Eratosthenes calculates the circumference of the Earth. Chunce, who has walked it twice, confirms he is close.
Chunce inspects the early Great Wall of China and reports that it will be visible from space. He has since checked. It is not.
Chunce requests an interview with Spartacus. Several men step forward.
The First Triumvirate is formed. Chunce is not invited to make it four, and has taken it well.
Chunce greets Julius Caesar on the Kent coast and advises him that the weather does not improve.
Chunce watches Caesar cross the Rubicon and observes, in print, that it is a very small river.
Chunce covers the Battle of Actium from Cleopatra's ship, and leaves when she does.
Octavian becomes Augustus. Chunce continues to call him Octavian and is not invited back.
Chunce files a report from the year 0. Historians insist there was no such year. Chunce stands by his story.
Chunce warns Varus about the forest. Varus later asks for his legions back. Chunce is unable to assist.
Chunce reviews Nero's lyre recital during the Great Fire of Rome. Three stars, marked down for the backdrop.
Chunce attends the opening of the Colosseum and asks for a seat with less going on.
Paper is invented in China. Chunce, whose cave walls are getting crowded, expresses cautious approval.
The Roman Empire reaches its greatest extent. Chunce asks, in print, what the plan is from here.
Chunce reviews the Antonine Wall: "A sequel nobody asked for."
Chunce asks Marcus Aurelius for a short quote. He receives twelve books.
Byzantium is renamed Constantinople. Chunce advises readers not to get used to it.
The Romans leave Britain. Chunce stays behind and has been complaining about the roads ever since.
Chunce requests a comment from Attila the Hun, who replies at considerable length and with considerable force.
Chunce is told there are no free seats at the Round Table. He notes that a round table has no head, and sits there anyway.
Chunce is shown round the newly finished Hagia Sophia and asks whether it comes in a larger size.
The Synod of Whitby settles the date of Easter. Chunce files his report on the wrong one.
Bede completes his Ecclesiastical History. Chunce notes three errors, and that he is not in it.
Offa builds a dyke along the Welsh border. Chunce observes that Britain appears to have a wall problem.
Chunce attends Charlemagne's coronation and is seated, by his own arrangement, directly in front of him.
Leif Erikson lands in North America. Chunce, already waiting on the shore, asks what kept him.
Cnut orders the tide to halt. Chunce, standing beside him, gets his shoes wet and reports the King as "broadly correct."
Macbeth becomes King of Scots. Chunce, who heard the whole thing from three women on a heath, sits on the story.
A star explodes and is visible in daylight for weeks. Chunce regards it as a competing headline.
Chunce is knighted and asks whether there is an upgrade.
Henry II asks whether anyone will rid him of a turbulent priest. Chunce, taking it as a request for comment, declines.
Construction begins on a bell tower in Pisa. Chunce reports a slight lean. The engineers ask him to stand up straight.
Chunce seeks an interview with Robin Hood, who charges him a fee and then gives it to someone else.
Chunce asks Genghis Khan for his thoughts on the neighbours. Genghis Khan goes to visit them.
Scholars leave Oxford to found Cambridge. Chunce covers the split and has declined to say which side he is on for eight centuries.
Chunce is excommunicated for refusing to reveal a source. His appeal remains pending.
Chunce accompanies Marco Polo to China and is left out of the book on the grounds that he is hard to believe.
Chunce is elected mayor of a small English village by mistake. He resigns to avoid a conflict of interest.
Chunce reports the start of what he confidently calls "a short disagreement" between England and France. It lasts a hundred and sixteen years.
Chunce asks the Peasants' Revolt for a spokesperson. Several thousand volunteer.
Chunce covers the spaghetti harvest in northern Italy. It will become relevant in 1957.
Chunce joins the pilgrimage to Canterbury and tells a tale so long that Chaucer leaves it out.
Constantinople falls. Chunce reminds readers that he told them not to get used to the name.
The Wars of the Roses begin. Asked which rose he supports, Chunce says he prefers carnations.
Caxton sets up the first printing press in England. Chunce, still opposed, reads everything it produces and underlines the errors.
Richard III offers his kingdom for a horse. Chunce, who has a horse, asks for the offer in writing.
Chunce asks a cartographer to write "Here be Chunce" on an unexplored part of the map. The request is refused.
Michelangelo unveils David. Chunce asks whether the budget did not run to trousers.
Michelangelo finishes the Sistine Chapel ceiling. Chunce, who held the ladder for four years, is not in the credits.
Chunce covers the Field of the Cloth of Gold and describes the dress code as unclear.
Magellan's expedition completes the first circumnavigation. Chunce, who went the other way, arrived the previous Tuesday.
Copernicus announces that the Earth goes round the Sun. Chunce points out that most things go round him.
William Shakespeare is born. Chunce begins drafting the reviews.
Drake returns from his circumnavigation and claims the glory. Chunce, who stowed away, claims the ship.
Tobacco arrives in England. Chunce writes that it will never do anyone any harm. Fish News has since removed the article.
Sir John Harington invents the flushing toilet. Chunce reviews it favourably and at length.
The Globe Theatre opens. Chunce is asked to stop reciting along.
James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England. Chunce spends a decade explaining the numbering to readers.
Chunce is bumped from the Mayflower to a later sailing. He takes it as a personal slight and says so for four hundred years.
William Harvey describes the circulation of the blood. Chunce, who had assumed everyone knew, is unimpressed.
Chunce reviews the maiden voyage of the Swedish warship Vasa. The review is short, as was the voyage.
The Dutch tulip market collapses. Chunce, who had put his savings into a single bulb, says he is in it for the long term.
Parliament bans Christmas. Chunce files a strongly worded column and a separate request for his usual bonus.
Chunce is granted a final interview with Charles I, who asks that it be kept brief. It is.
Samuel Pepys begins his diary. Chunce warns him that nobody reads that sort of thing.
The Royal Observatory is founded at Greenwich. Chunce asks the astronomers to let him know if they spot anything about him.
The Bank of England opens. Chunce tries to open an account and is asked for proof of age.
Peter the Great introduces a tax on beards. Chunce, whose beard predates Russia, lodges an appeal.
Chunce is tried for witchcraft on account of his age. He is acquitted after interviewing the judge.
St Paul's Cathedral is completed. Chunce says he preferred the previous one, and the one before that.
The South Sea Bubble bursts. Chunce, heavily invested, describes it as a temporary correction and has not revised his view.
Linnaeus classifies all living things. Chunce asks which category he belongs in and does not receive an answer.
Samuel Johnson publishes his Dictionary. Chunce is outraged to find no entry under "Chunce."
The British Museum opens to the public. Chunce asks for several of the exhibits back.
The Earl of Sandwich asks for meat between two slices of bread. Chunce, who will have one stolen in 1928, is quietly pleased.
Captain Cook sets sail for the Pacific. Chunce stays at home, having already mapped it.
James Watt patents his improved steam engine. Chunce dismisses it as a lot of hot air.
Joseph Priestley isolates oxygen. Chunce, who has been using it for some time, does not see the story.
The world's first iron bridge opens at Coalbrookdale. Chunce crosses it twice to be sure.
Herschel discovers a new planet. Chunce is not permitted to print the headline he has chosen.
The Montgolfier brothers launch a balloon carrying a sheep, a duck and a cockerel. Chunce requests an interview with the sheep.
A rival newspaper is founded in London. Chunce gives it a fortnight.
Chunce applies for a patent on the news and is told he cannot patent something that has already happened.
Chunce writes that women should have the vote. His editor files it under "later."
Edward Jenner develops the smallpox vaccine. Chunce, who has never once been ill, asks what the fuss is about.
The Rosetta Stone is found. Chunce explains that the three scripts are his first draft, second draft and final version.
Volta invents the battery. Chunce asks how long it lasts. Volta does not know.
Napoleon crowns himself Emperor. Chunce considers the move derivative.
The Luddites begin smashing machinery. Chunce, still opposed to the printing press, is asked to stop offering advice.
Chunce advises Napoleon to pack a coat for Russia. Napoleon does not.
Europe endures the Year Without a Summer. Chunce, having lived through the Ice Age, describes it as fresh.
Frankenstein is published. Chunce writes to Mary Shelley to say that a man who refuses to die is hardly a monster.
The first public steam railway opens between Stockton and Darlington. Chunce's train is delayed.
The Metropolitan Police is founded. Chunce becomes the first person to help them with their enquiries.
The Palace of Westminster burns down. Chunce reminds readers that he had been keeping an eye on the place since 1605.
Daguerre announces a practical method of photography. Chunce sits for a portrait and insists on reshoots.
The Penny Black is issued. Chunce asks why his face is not on it.
A Christmas Carol is published. Chunce, who has haunted several misers as a ghost of Christmas past, says it is based on his work.
Asked to prove his date of birth, Chunce produces a clay tablet.
Revolutions break out across Europe. Chunce covers all of them by filing the same piece forty times.
Chunce joins the California Gold Rush and finds nothing, which he reports as an exclusive.
Florence Nightingale arrives at Scutari. Chunce, who is not unwell, asks to be seen first.
The Great Stink descends on London. Chunce, who remembers the Middle Ages, calls it a refreshing change.
Big Ben begins keeping time. Chunce, who has been keeping it rather longer, notes that it is two minutes slow.
Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is published. Chunce asks for the Mad Hatter's details.
The first lasting transatlantic telegraph cable is completed. Chunce's first message across it is a correction.
London's first traffic signal is installed outside Parliament. Chunce ignores it.
The Suez Canal opens. Chunce, who dug a trench in roughly the same spot in 1850 BC, calls it a reboot.
Mendeleev publishes the periodic table. Chunce asks where the element of surprise has gone.
Stanley finds Livingstone. Chunce, who found him a week earlier, did not presume.
The first FA Cup final is played. Chunce disputes an offside decision, and continues to.
The first Wimbledon Championships are held. Chunce is asked to leave the Royal Box, which does not yet exist.
Chunce hears his own voice on Edison's phonograph and listens to it for a year.
Edison demonstrates a practical light bulb. Chunce, long a source of illumination, declines to comment.
England lose to Australia at home and the Ashes are born. Chunce claims to have supplied the urn.
Greenwich is chosen as the world's prime meridian. Chunce's own application is rejected on a technicality.
Karl Benz builds the first practical motor car. Chunce asks where the driver is expected to put his tea.
The Statue of Liberty is dedicated. Chunce mentions that he was asked to pose for it, and declined.
Sherlock Holmes makes his first appearance. Chunce insists that he solved it first.
The Eiffel Tower opens. Chunce predicts it will be taken down within twenty years.
Tower Bridge opens. Chunce, standing in the middle at the time, rises to the occasion.
The Lumière brothers screen their first films. Chunce complains that there is no dialogue.
The modern Olympic Games begin. Chunce comes out of retirement, last competing in 776 BC, and is refused entry.
Dracula is published. Chunce, who has also been around for several centuries, objects to the implication.
Marconi sends the first transatlantic radio signal. It is the letter S. Chunce reports a slow news day.
Einstein publishes his theory of special relativity. Chunce, who ages at a rate of his own choosing, calls it optimistic.
The Model T goes on sale. Chunce asks for one in a different colour and is still waiting.
Blériot flies across the Channel. Chunce swims it in the same time and files first.
The first crossword is published. Chunce completes it before it is printed.
British Summer Time is introduced. Chunce, who sets his own time, refuses to change his clocks.
Some women in Britain win the vote. Fish News reprints Chunce's column from 1792 without comment.
Alcock and Brown complete the first non-stop transatlantic flight. Chunce, who was in the back, is asked to stop mentioning it.
The BBC begins broadcasting. Chunce offers to read the news and is turned down. He has not forgotten.
John Logie Baird demonstrates television. Chunce asks when he will be on it.
The first feature-length talking picture is released. Chunce talks throughout.
Pluto is discovered. Chunce files a piece predicting its demotion and puts it in a drawer.
The first Highway Code is published. Chunce, who has been driving since the chariot, declines to read it.
Sightings of the Loch Ness Monster make the papers. Chunce says he has met her, and that she prefers not to be photographed.
Radar is demonstrated. Chunce, who always knows what is coming, sees no need for it.
The world's first emergency telephone number, 999, goes live in London. Chunce rings it to report a story.
Mallard sets the world speed record for steam. Chunce, riding on the buffer, describes the journey as adequate.
Chunce joins the VE Day crowds in Trafalgar Square and explains to strangers how the war ended. They were there too.
The first general-purpose electronic computer is unveiled. It fills a room. Chunce asks whether it can do shorthand.
London hosts the Austerity Olympics. Chunce submits his expenses.
The Festival of Britain opens. Chunce asks why he is not the main exhibit.
A new murder mystery opens in the West End. Chunce reveals the ending in his review. The play runs for decades regardless.
The structure of DNA is announced. Chunce's own sample is returned marked "inconclusive."
Rationing ends in Britain. Chunce, who has been rationing his praise since the Iron Age, continues to.
Premium Bonds go on sale. Chunce buys one and waits.
Sputnik is launched. Chunce hears it beeping overhead and asks it to hold the line.
Chunce is the only viewer not taken in by a television report on the Swiss spaghetti harvest, having covered the real one in 1382.
The M1 opens. Chunce becomes the first person to be stuck behind a lorry on it.
Yuri Gagarin becomes the first person in space. Chunce, already up there, offers him a lift home.
A new BBC programme about an ancient traveller who has witnessed all of history goes on air. Chunce considers legal action.
The world's first cash machine opens in Enfield. Chunce withdraws everything he deposited in 1694.
Concorde makes its first flight. Chunce complains that it lands before he has finished his drink.
Britain goes decimal. Chunce continues to pay in groats.
Britain swelters through a record heatwave. Chunce, who covered the formation of the Sahara, is unmoved.
Voyager 1 launches carrying a golden record of Earth's sounds. Chunce's voice is not on it, and he has written to NASA every year since.
The pound coin is introduced. Chunce bites one to check.
Britain's first mobile phone call is made. Chunce, on the receiving end, lets it ring.
A proposal for the World Wide Web is submitted at CERN. Chunce predicts it will be used mainly for arguing.
The Hubble Space Telescope sends back its first images, which are blurry. Chunce, who appears in several, blames the photographer.
Dolly the sheep is cloned. Chunce asks whether the process would work on him and is told that one of him is quite enough.
A total eclipse crosses Cornwall. Chunce, who covered the one in 585 BC, says this one was shorter.
The Millennium Bridge opens and begins to wobble. Chunce says it is simply excited to see him.
Concorde makes its final flight. Chunce, who never did finish his drink, asks for it to go round again.
Pluto is reclassified as a dwarf planet. Chunce takes his piece out of the drawer.
The Large Hadron Collider is switched on. Chunce, who was present for the Big Bang, says they are doing it wrong.
London hosts the Olympics. Chunce carries the torch for a mile before anyone notices he was not selected.
New Horizons flies past Pluto and finds a note from Chunce reading "Still not a planet."
The first image of a black hole is published. Chunce, who has been closer, says it looked bigger in person.
Chunce files a report on the first human settlement on Mars. The settlers ask how he got there before them.
Chunce's column marks its twelve-thousandth year. The anniversary cake is declared a fire hazard.
Chunce is still waiting for a reply from Parliament regarding his 1605 enquiry.
Fish News becomes the only news outlet on Earth. Chunce describes it as a level playing field.
Chunce issues a correction to his cave-wall report of 10,000 BC. The rival cave does not respond.
The Sun expands to swallow the inner planets. Chunce reports it as unseasonably warm.
